title: Typing Map, Set, and Weak collections
hook: Map<K,V> and Set<T> are ES2015 collections with generic type parameters — unlike plain objects, they accept any key type and preserve insertion order. WeakMap and WeakSet only hold object keys and do not prevent garbage collection.

blocks.text: **Map<K, V>** stores key-value pairs where `K` can be any type (string, number, object reference). **Set<T>** stores unique values of type `T`. **WeakMap<K extends object, V>** and **WeakSet<T extends object>** hold only object keys/values and do not enumerate — entries disappear when the key object is garbage-collected. TypeScript generics on these classes give compile-time safety for `.get()`, `.set()`, and iteration. At runtime they are native ES2015 collections; types erase completely.

entries.plainDefinition: Key-value collection with any key type and O(1) lookup by reference or primitive.
Collection of unique values — duplicates ignored by SameValueZero equality.
Map with object-only keys; no size property, not iterable — keys can be GC'd.
Set/Map equality: NaN equals NaN, +0 equals -0.

blocks.text: Use `Map` when keys are not strings or when you need reliable iteration order — DOM node metadata, memoization caches keyed by object identity. `Record<string, T>` only accepts string keys and cannot use objects as keys. `Set` deduplicates IDs in ETL pipelines. `WeakMap` attaches private metadata to DOM nodes without leaking memory — when the node is removed, the WeakMap entry vanishes. C# has `Dictionary<K,V>` and `HashSet<T>` with full generic constraints; TypeScript's Map/Set are structural wrappers with no compile-time key constraint beyond extends object for Weak collections.

blocks.title: Map vs Record
blocks.body: Record<string, T> for JSON-shaped config with known string keys. Map<K,V> for dynamic keys, non-string keys, or frequent add/delete.

blocks.title: Using plain object as Map substitute
blocks.body: Object keys are always strings (or symbols). Object keys coerce — Map preserves key identity for objects.

blocks.title: Expecting WeakMap iteration
blocks.body: WeakMap has no keys(), values(), or size — by design for GC. Use Map if you need enumeration.

blocks.text: Map uses SameValueZero — `map.set(NaN, 1)` and `map.get(NaN)` work. Object keys in Map are compared by reference, not deep equality. ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet interfaces allow passing immutable views. For concurrent access, JS Map is not thread-safe (unlike C# ConcurrentDictionary) — use workers with message passing. Serialization: Map/Set do not JSON.stringify natively — convert to entries array first.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Object keys, insertion order, frequent mutation
No index access — must convert to array

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain Map.get returns undefined. Thinking WeakMap prevents GC of values (only keys are weak). Using Record when object reference keys are needed.

interviewTakeaways: Map<K,V> — any key type, insertion order, get returns T | undefined.
Set<T> — unique values via SameValueZero; NaN dedupes.
WeakMap/WeakSet — object keys only, not iterable, GC-friendly.
60s: Map for dynamic or object keys. Record for string-keyed JSON shape. WeakMap for per-object metadata without leaks. Always handle undefined from get.
Follow-up: ReadonlyMap, serialization to JSON, Map vs C# Dictionary thread safety.
commonPitfalls: Weak: "Map is just a typed object" — key identity and iteration differ.
Ignoring undefined from Map.get under strictNullChecks.
Strong: "Map preserves key reference equality. WeakMap for metadata on objects. get always returns T | undefined."

jsTsCorrelations.note: ES2015 Map/Set are identical at runtime — TypeScript adds generic parameters for compile-time key/value typing.
C# Dictionary<K,V> enforces K : notnull and uses GetHashCode; TS Map accepts any K with no constraint clause.
